newsitem.title: UK: Full text of March 5 UK monetary minutes.
newsitem.headline: Full text of March 5 UK monetary minutes.

text.p: The following is the complete text of the minutes of the March 5 monthly monetary policy meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Governor of the Bank of England met, together with officials, on 5 March, to review monetary developments.
Monetary and Economic Developments
2. Latest monetary and economic data (reviewed by

officials before the meeting) confirmed that cost pressures remained weak, despite the tightening labour market. There were continuing signs that activity remained strong, and concentrated on the consumer side.
Inflation Indicators
3. Underlying inflation (RPI excluding mortgage interest

payments - RPIX) was unchanged as expected in January, at 3.1 per cent. However, all-items RPI inflation rose by 0.3 percentage points, to 2.8 per cent, due largely to an increase in mortgage interest payments following the delayed response of building societies to October's base rate rise.
4. Most indicators confirmed that cost pressures remained
weak:
- sterling non-oil commodity prices rose by 0.4 per cent in January, but were 5.0 per cent lower than a year ago. The oil price had fallen again sharply to $19.4 per barrel;
- sterling's effective exchange rate index had risen further from 96.1 before the last meeting, to 98.1 currently;

- total non-oil import prices fell by 2.8 per cent in the three months to December compared to the previous three months, and were 4.0 per cent lower than a year ago. Non-EU import prices fell by 4.4 per cent in the three months to January on the previous three months;

- producer input prices for manufacturing (excluding food, beverage, tobacco and petroleum industries) fell in January by 0.3 per cent; and compared to a year ago they were 7.8 per cent lower. The CIPS survey input price indicator also fell again in February;

- producer output prices (excluding FBTP) fell by 0.1 per cent in January; and the annual inflation rate fell to 0.6 per cent, from 0.8 per cent in December. The CBI survey output price expectations balance fell in February;

- the annual growth rate of underlying average earnings was unchanged in December, at 4-1/4 per cent (following February's upward revision to the November figure); and IRS median pay settlements were also unchanged at 3.0 per cent in January.
Monetary and Financial Indicators
5. Notes and coin grew by 0.2 per cent in February,
following a 0.7 per cent rise in January; and the annual growth rate fell to 6.4 per cent. M0's annual growth rate also fell, to 6.5 per cent.
6. M4 grew by 1.6 per cent in January, after falling by
0.4 per cent in December. The annual growth rate of M4 and M4 lending rose, to 9.8 per cent, and 8.9 per cent, respectively.
7. The Halifax house price index rose by 0.5 per cent in

February, giving an annual increase of 6.8 per cent. The Nationwide index rose by 0.7 per cent in February, and was 8.5 per cent up on a year earlier. Housing market transactions continued to grow strongly; in the three months to January particulars delivered (which lag actual transactions) were 10.7 per cent up on the previous three months, and 31.3 per cent higher than a year earlier.
8. Short-term interest rates were little changed in the US

and Japan since the last meeting, but had risen by nearly 10 basis points in Germany. In contrast, UK short-term interest rates had fallen by around 10 basis points; and forward rates implicit in short-sterling futures contracts had fallen (by less than 20 basis points) at all maturities.
9. 10-year bond yields had risen (by less than 10 basis

points) in the US and Japan, but had fallen by almost 30 basis points in Germany. In the UK, yields on conventional gilts had fallen at all maturities (by up to 12 basis points). Since the last meeting inflation expectations implied by the gilt yield curve (calculated by the Bank from the difference between the yields on conventional and index-linked bonds) were little changed for 5 years ahead, and had fallen by less than 10 basis points for 10 years ahead.
Activity Indicators

10. In the US recent data confirmed that output was growing at around trend. However, GDP grew more strongly than expected in Q4, by 1.0 per cent (not annualised), following growth of 0.5 per cent in Q3, leaving it 2.4 per cent up on a year earlier. Industrial production was unchanged in January, following a rise of 0.5 per cent in December. In Japan industrial production rose by 5.3 per cent in January, following a rise of 0.1 per cent in December.

11. In Germany the latest estimate of GDP growth in Q4 was 0.1 per cent, leaving it 1.4 per cent up on a year earlier. But industrial production fell by 1.7 per cent in January, following a rise of 0.8 per cent in December. Unemployment rose sharply in January to a new high of 11.3 per cent (although the rise was exaggerated by administrative changes). In France unemployment fell slightly in January, but remained at a high of 12.7 per cent.

12. The latest estimate of UK GDP growth in Q4 showed that whole economy and non-oil GDP grew by 0.8 per cent and 0.7 per cent respectively, and were respectively 2.7 per cent and 2.5 per cent up on a year earlier. Consumer spending rose by 0.9 per cent in Q4, leaving it 3.7 per cent up on a year earlier. Investment rose by 0.2 per cent in Q4, and net trade made a positive contribution to growth.
13. Most other activity data were consistent with output growth continuing above trend, although indicators of business confidence were more mixed:

- manufacturing output rose by 0.2 per cent in December, and in the three months to December it was up 0.9 per cent on a year earlier. Total industrial output rose by 0.6 per cent in December, and in the latest three months was up 1.7 per cent on a year earlier;

- major business surveys continued to suggest continuing growth in activity, although at a slower rate than in previous months. The February CIPS and CBI surveys both showed a rise in output indicators for manufacturing, but the CIPS survey showed weaker orders;

- retail sales volumes rose by 0.6 per cent in January; and in the latest three months they rose by 0.9 per cent compared to the previous three months, and were 3.9 per cent higher than a year earlier;

- and latest survey indicators in the retail sector showed continuing sales growth: consumer confidence rose in February to its highest level since August 1988; the January CBI Distributive Trades Survey showed a slight rise in the balance of retailers expecting higher sales; and the January BRC survey showed a pick-up In sales growth;

- claimant unemployment fell by 67,800 in January, to its lowest level since November 1990 (although the fall was exaggerated by the introduction of the Job Seekers Allowance). The Autumn Labour Force Survey showed a much smaller fall in unemployment (down 32,000 in the quarter), although employment rose by 130,000, virtually all full-time jobs. Unfilled vacancies at Jobcentres fell by 3,500 in January, but remained on a strong upward trend.
Summary of discussion

14. The Governor said that since the last meeting a month ago both the monetary data and the activity indicators had perked up - confirming, as the Bank had supposed, that the apparent softening at the end of last year was in fact erratic. So the underlying picture was much as it had been. Inflationary pressure was - and was likely to remain - weak in the short term, with the strong exchange rate helping to hold down costs and prices, at the manufacturing producer level particularly. But the persistence of rapid monetary growth and above-trend growth of consumer demand and overall output represented a developing threat to the inflation target as we moved through next year.

15. Looking first at the short-term prospect, the encouraging news on inflation continued. Cost pressures early in the supply chain were very subdued. Sterling commodity prices (excluding oil) were some 5-1/2 per cent lower in January than a year before; and crude oil prices had fallen sharply (by 3 per cent in sterling terms) in the past two months.

16. The Governor noted that costs in manufacturing were notably weak. Input prices had fallen for the third successive month in January - to 6.3 per cent below a year ago (7.8 per cent lower ex FBTP). And despite higher average earnings growth (4-3/4 per cent over the year to December) the rise in unit labour costs in manufacturing had moderated for the present at least (annual growth of 3.2 per cent on average in the 3 months to December compared with 4.7 per cent in the three months to September) with productivity improving as output growth had recovered. Manufacturing output prices had also fallen, unusually, in January (after seasonal adjustment); and excluding excise duties they had in fact now fallen over the past three months. Over the past year output prices had risen by only 1.5 per cent - the smallest annual rise since 1986.

17. At the retail level, annual RPIX inflation had remained unchanged in January at 3.1 per cent. Annual goods price inflation had fallen slightly, from 2.7 per cent to 2.6 per cent, but service sector inflation had risen from 3.0 per cent to 3.2 per cent. The Bank nevertheless still expected RPIX inflation to come down during the coming months as the effect of sterling's appreciation and lower producer price inflation worked their way through, though the speed and extent of this pass through was necessarily uncertain. That much was encouraging.

18. But, the Governor said, policy of course needed to look beyond the short term, and the prospect for inflation further ahead depended essentially on the pressure of demand, which continued gradually to build.

19. Monetary growth had bounced back strongly in January, having been depressed in December by end-year factors. Both M4 and M4 lending had grown by over 1-1/2 per cent on the month, leaving underlying 12-month growth at around 8-10 per cent where it had been fairly consistently now for the past 18 months. Narrow money growth (notes and coin) had also recovered in January (to 0.7 per cent) but this had not been sustained in February (0.2 per cent).

20. Turning to output, revised GDP estimates for Q4 had confirmed total output growth at 0.8 per cent - an annualised rate of 3 per cent in H2 which was well above any reasonable estimate of trend growth. Both services and industrial production had grown by 0.9 per cent in Q4, and construction growth was particularly strong at 1.1 per cent, the highest quarterly rate for over 2 years.

21. On the monthly data manufacturing output had risen by 0.2 per cent in December after falling by 0.4 per cent in November. Manufacturing output therefore had risen by 0.6 per cent overall in Q4, the same rate as in Q3. The February survey evidence (from CBI and CIPS surveys) suggested continuing growth of output, though with some weakening of export orders.

22. The Governor noted that, reflecting the growth of output, the labour market continued to tighten - even though the extent of the underlying tightening was perhaps being somewhat exaggerated by claimant unemployment. Average earnings growth had picked up - to 4-3/4 per cent in the private sector, the highest rate since November 1992 - which may have reflected bonus payments, particularly in the financial sector. Pay settlements, on the other hand, appeared relatively stable at 3-1/2 per cent or perhaps somewhat less.

23. On the demand side, the running continued to be made by consumer spending, which had risen by 0.9 per cent in Q4, or at an annualised rate of just over 3-3/4 per cent in H2 - again well above trend. Total investment had grown by only 0.2 per cent in Q4, but within that business investment had risen by over 3 per cent. Net external trade perhaps surprisingly had made a small positive contribution to GDP growth (+0.2 per cent) in Q4.
24. And, the Governor said, the growth of demand appeared to be continuing.

25. Retail sales volumes had recovered in January (up 0.6 per cent) after the December fall, pushing the annualised growth rate (3 months on 3 months a year earlier) up to 3.9 per cent. And the recovery in the housing market continued - with Halifax house prices recovering in February after the erratic fall in January.

26. The outlook for business fixed investment also remained favourable: profitability had improved with trading profits at nearly 16 per cent of GDP in Q4 - the highest level since 1989 Q1. And notwithstanding the survey evidence on export prospects, exports were so far holding up surprisingly well - with the unexpectedly large fall in export volumes to the non-EU countries in December more than reversed in January.

27. The Governor said that, taking the monetary data and the demand and output data together, the likelihood was, in the Bank's view, that the economy would continue to grow above trend under the impact of domestic - particularly consumer - demand. This would in due course put upward pressure on inflation unless action was taken to slow the growth of demand to a sustainable pace.

28. The Bank recognised of course the effect of the exchange rate in restraining inflation, particularly in the short term, and the real dilemma which sterling's effective appreciation posed for policy. But there was very little that could be done about that directly through monetary policy. The fact that sterling had actually depreciated over the past two months against the dollar while appreciating further against the European currencies suggested that it was largely a function of developments abroad.

29. The policy judgement was of course, as always, a matter of balancing risks. But the Bank's concern was that, if, on account of the exchange rate, the necessary tightening of policy to moderate the pace of the domestic expansion was delayed, then more substantial tightening would eventually become unavoidable. The Bank continued to advise therefore that interest rates be raised now by 1/4 per cent.

30. The Chancellor said that there was general agreement that the outlook had not changed much since the previous meeting. Inflation was expected to fall below the target of 2-1/2 per cent or less by the end of this year. The prospects for inflation in 1998 and beyond were more uncertain, but the evidence on this had not moved decisively one way or the other since the previous meeting.

31. The Chancellor said that consumer demand was growing at a strong but sustainable rate. Consumers were still cautious and competition among retailers remained strong, especially among the supermarkets. Food price inflation had been close to zero over the previous six months.

32. Since the previous meeting the exchange rate had risen slightly further again. The effect of the rise in the exchange rate since last summer was already apparent in the producer prices figures. In time, it would also have a significant effect on output, especially in manufacturing. The Chancellor said that no one was certain why the pound had strengthened so much. He agreed that policy should not be set in order to influence the exchange rate, but movements in the exchange rate could not be ignored either since they had an impact on the outlook for inflation.

33. The Chancellor noted that the further estimate of GDP, published since the previous meeting, had confirmed non-oil GDP growth of 0.7 per cent in the fourth quarter. Consumer spending had grown by 0.9 per cent, arguably a little above trend but not unsustainable. In the three months to January retail sales were 3.9 per cent up on a year earlier. The housing market remained buoyant. The building society price indices showed house price inflation at 7 to 8-1/2 per cent a year. A shortage of properties was pushing house price inflation up temporarily, but housing starts had picked up and would lead to an increase in supply.

34. The Chancellor said that the stronger exchange rate was beginning to have an effect on expectations about export prospects, and also about prices. Although industry surveys still revealed comparative optimism among manufacturers, this could not last indefinitely.

35. The stronger exchange rate was clearly having an effect on producer prices, which remained extremely subdued. Underlying output prices were 0.6 per cent up on a year ago in January, compared to 0.8 per cent in the year to December. Input prices continued to fall, and were 7.8 per cent lower than a year ago.

36. The Chancellor said that the labour market was still recovering strongly, and the claimant count measure of unemployment was falling rapidly. This was likely to overstate the fall because of the introduction of the Job Seekers Allowance, and on the Labour Force Survey measure the rate of decline in unemployment was less steep. The improving labour market had still had very little effect on pay settlements, which remained around 3 per cent on average. Earnings growth was unchanged at 4-1/4 per cent in December, and reflected good bonus payments in the financial sector.

37. The monetary data were pointing in different directions. M4 growth rose slightly in January, from an annual rate of 9.5 per cent to 9.8 per cent. M0 growth, on the other hand, had fallen back in February.

38. The Chancellor said that, in his view, the upside and downside risks associated with the prospect for inflation two years out were very balanced. Since the last meeting, the upside risk of unsustainably strong consumer demand had eased somewhat. And the exchange rate had strengthened further.
39. In discussion the following points were made:
- while the risk of very strong activity growth in the
near term had diminished, the most likely outlook for growth this year could still be inconsistent with inflation remaining below 2-1/2 per cent through 1998;
- if the exchange rate remained very high, this would have

a deflationary effect. But its main effect on inflation would be relatively short-term and temporary (as the effect of lower oil prices had been in the mid-1980s). There was a strong case for not offsetting this temporary effect, even if inflation fell significantly below 2-1/2 per cent for a time;
- the labour market continued to tighten. Average earnings

growth had risen significantly from its trough of 3-1/4 per cent at the end of 1995 to 4-1/4 per cent in December, with particularly strong rises in the private sector and in services. If earnings accelerated further, they could soon reach a level that was inconsistent with meeting the inflation target in the medium term;
- on the other hand, there were factors moderating

earnings pressures: the labour market was now much more flexible; job insecurity was a factor moderating wage demands (although this effect may be only a temporary one); and RPI inflation was falling. Also the recent Pay Review Body recommendations would result in an average pay increase for those public sector groups of less than 2-1/2 per cent.
Conclusion

40. In summary, the Chancellor said that not a great deal had changed since the last meeting. The extra information had not justified a change in view. So he and the Governor remained a 1/4 percentage point apart in their views on the appropriate level of interest rates. This reflected a small difference of judgment about the outlook for inflation 1-2 years ahead, and about the balance of risks. He decided to leave interest rates unchanged for the moment.
H M Treasury
